result.summary: Pindar says his song, unlike a statue, travels by ship to announce that Pytheas of Aigina won the boys' pankration at Nemea. He praises the Aiakidai and Aigina, hints at a dark deed of Peleus and Telamon and breaks off, then sings the Muses' tale of Peleus resisting Hippolyte and winning Thetis, before praising Pytheas's kin and trainer.

scenes.title: Song sails forth for Pytheas
scenes.summary: Pindar announces Pytheas's Nemean victory and honours the Aiakidai and Aigina, recalling their ancestors' prayer at the altar of Zeus Hellenios.

scenes.title: Pindar breaks off
scenes.summary: Pindar refuses to tell of the heroes' crime and exile, saying silence is often wisest, and turns to other praise.

scenes.title: The Muses sing of Peleus
scenes.summary: On Pelion the Muses and Apollo sing how Peleus refused Hippolyte's advances, was slandered, and was rewarded by Zeus with the Nereid Thetis through Poseidon.
scenes.stakes: Peleus risks false accusation and the wrath of Zeus if he betrays his host.

scenes.title: Praise of Pytheas's kin
scenes.summary: Pindar honours Euthymenes, Pytheas, his uncle Themistios and trainer Menander, and urges singing of Themistios's victories.

notable_quotes.reason: Famous opening contrasting travelling song with static statues.
Memorable reflection that silence is sometimes wisest.

analysis.text: Poetry is presented as mobile and lasting, spreading athletic fame beyond the island, while the myth of Peleus's restraint models virtue rewarded.
Epinikian odes honoured victors and their families, and tied Aigina's civic pride to the local Aiakid heroes.

fun_facts.text: The opening line is often cited as a comparison between poetry and sculpture, though Pindar's song was meant for choral performance.

language_notes.text: The 'vine-bloom's mother, mellowing midsummer' is a periphrasis for the first beard; Pytheas is still beardless, so very young.
Pankratiast: a competitor in the pankration, a brutal combined boxing and wrestling contest.
Aiakidai: the descendants of Aiakos, the legendary heroes of Aigina, including Peleus, Telamon and Achilles.
The 'deed portentous' is the killing of Phokos by his half-brothers Peleus and Telamon, which led to their exile from Aigina. Pindar declines to name it.
Oinone: an older name for Aigina.
Hippolyte, wife of Akastos, falsely accused Peleus of trying to seduce her after he rejected her advances.
Nereids: sea-nymphs, daughters of Nereus. Thetis was one of them.
Poseidon was worshipped at the Isthmian games near Corinth, the 'Dorian Isthmus', where contests were held in his honour.
Athens is praised as the source of a good trainer; Menander was an Athenian.

context_notes.text: Zeus Hellenios was a cult title of Zeus on Aigina. Aiakos, father of Peleus and Telamon, was said to have prayed to him there.
Pelion is the mountain in Thessaly where Peleus later married Thetis, with the Muses and Apollo singing at the wedding.
Euthymenes was an earlier family victor, probably Pytheas's maternal grandfather. 'Thy mother's brother' refers to Pytheas's uncle Themistios.

literary_notes.text: Pindar's song is imagined as a traveller sailing on merchant ships, contrasting poetry's mobility with a static statue.
Pindar abruptly breaks off the myth, using silence itself as a way to hint at the unspeakable crime.
The poet as a leaping athlete with nimble knees, and the eagles flying over the sea, convey his ease in moving to a new theme.
Peleus's refusal out of respect for Zeus, protector of host and guest, shows his piety and self-restraint.
A short general maxim about inborn fate sums up the myth and prepares the turn to the victors.
Hoisting the sail to the mast-top means praising boldly, extending the ship imagery from the opening.
